extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, practicing scientists, and graduate students interested in the nature and practice of scientific research
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the features, functions, and consequences of scientific paradigms and 'normal science'—how paradigms shape research problems, methods, communication, and instrument design across mature sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm as criterion of a science
rubrics_metrics.description: A field achieves the status of a science when a paradigm capable of guiding the whole group's research has been achieved; 'They had ... achieved a paradigm that proved able to guide the whole group's research.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paradigm is identified by its ability to direct the research agenda of a professional group, enabling practitioners to take foundational assumptions for granted. With hindsight, achieving such a paradigm is a clear indicator that a field has become a science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm's initial limited scope and promise of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms at first are 'very limited in both scope and precision' and gain status because they are more successful than competitors in solving a few acute problems—a 'promise of success discoverable in selected and still incomplete examples.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a proposed paradigm not by universal coverage but by whether it demonstrably solves key, recognized problems better than alternatives; recognize that initial paradigms are partial and promise-driven rather than exhaustively successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science defined as articulation and actualization of a paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science consists in 'the actualization of that promise'—extending knowledge of facts the paradigm reveals, increasing match between those facts and the paradigm's predictions, and further articulation/specification of the paradigm itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess normal research by its contribution to extending, testing, refining, or articulating an accepted paradigm rather than by novelty. Successful normal-scientific work deepens or clarifies the paradigm's domain and its predictive precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research communication shifts with professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: As specialization and paradigms mature, researchers stop writing broad books and instead publish brief articles 'addressed only to professional colleagues' who share the paradigm and can 'read the papers addressed to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the intended audience and accessibility of publications as an indicator: a field whose primary research output is technical articles for insiders is typically operating under a mature paradigm; textbooks often codify paradigms for teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal scientists focus on 'mop‑up' or detailed, esoteric problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Most scientists engage in 'mop-up' operations—detailed, specialized investigations into narrow aspects of phenomena that the paradigm identifies as significant; these tasks occupy most careers and are essential to scientific progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and evaluate incremental, highly specialized work on its technical rigor, precision, and degree to which it deepens understanding within the paradigm; recognize such work as central, not marginal, to scientific development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for novelty versus adherence to paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science 'is not to call forth new sorts of phenomena' and 'scientists do not normally aim to invent new theories, and they are often intolerant of those invented by others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing work, distinguish between legitimate paradigm-driven research and attempts to challenge the paradigm; evaluate challenges by their evidence and consequences, but expect normal-science reviewers to be conservative about radical novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focal class 1 — determining paradigm‑significant facts
rubrics_metrics.description: One class of normal factual investigation targets facts the paradigm has shown to be 'particularly revealing of the nature of things' (e.g., stellar positions, specific gravities, combining weights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess empirical work on whether it improves precision, scope, or reliability of facts identified as central by the paradigm. Instrumentation, method development, and reproducibility are key evaluative subcriteria (examples: synchrotrons, radiotelescopes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focal class 2 — testing paradigm predictions (matching facts with theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second class seeks facts that can be directly compared with paradigm-theory predictions (e.g., experiments designed to test relativity, Atwood's machine for Newton's second law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate such work by the clarity of the theory–experiment contact: appropriateness of approximations, design sensitivity, and the degree to which the experiment discriminates between theoretical expectations and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focal class 3 — experiments to articulate and resolve paradigm ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: A third class conducts empirical work to 'articulate the paradigm theory,' resolving residual ambiguities and permitting solutions of newly posed problems (e.g., determining physical constants, distinguishing alternative applications of caloric theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether experiments are designed to address specific theoretical ambiguities, whether apparatus and methods are theory‑informed, and whether results refine, specify, or eliminate competing formulations of the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical problems mirror experimental classes (prediction, confrontation, articulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal theoretical work includes (a) using existing theory to predict useful factual information, (b) manipulating theory to create direct experimental contact, and (c) reformulating or clarifying theory to make it more coherent and applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review theoretical contributions for their usefulness in producing testable predictions, their role in making precise contact with data, and their success in clarifying or unifying existing formulations (examples: reformulations of Newtonian mechanics by Euler, Lagrange, Hamilton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science as puzzle‑solving with constrained expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science acts like puzzle-solving: problems typically 'aim to produce major novelties' rarely, and the 'typical latitude of expectation is only somewhat wider' than the paradigm allows; results outside that narrow range are often judged research failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating work, consider whether the outcomes fall within the range the paradigm makes intelligible; recognize that paradigm‑constrained expectations shape what counts as success or failure and that anomalous outcomes are exceptional but potentially significant.
